entries.narration: Data science is the craft of turning data into an answer you can trust, and then into something other people can use. This course teaches it by doing it once, properly, from start to finish, on one question that needs no explaining: what is this house worth? The six steps across the screen are the shape of almost every data science project, and they are the shape of this course. It starts with a question, specific enough to be answered. Then the data: a file of house sales, opened in a notebook, where you can look before you leap. Then cleaning, which is where most of the real work goes: every fault found, explained and fixed, and the fixes written down. Then exploring: grouping, joining and drawing the data, and learning to say how sure you are of anything you claim. Then a model that predicts a price, measured honestly against a baseline, and checked for the ways models fool you. And finally shipping: a tested package, a command, and a web service, so the answer outlives the notebook. Underneath are the tools, one for each job: Python, JupyterLab, pandas, NumPy and SciPy, scikit learn, pytest and FastAPI. All pinned to exact versions, and every output on screen in this course is real, produced by running the code.

Here is where we are going, before we take a single step. On the left is where it starts: data slash homes dot csv, fourteen hundred and sixty house sales from the town of Millbrook, over almost six years. It looks tidy in the first few lines. It is not. Somewhere in it are prices typed as text with pound signs, dates in two different formats, a batch of sizes in square metres, sales entered twice, and a few other surprises, every one of which we will find, explain and fix. In the middle is what we build along the way: seven notebooks where we explore, clean, measure and model, and then a proper Python package, house prices, with tests. On the right is where it ends. A command: ask it about a seventeen hundred and ten square foot house in Riverside, built in two thousand and four, with two garages, and it answers three hundred and eighty three thousand pounds, likely between three hundred and fifty and four hundred and seventeen thousand. Ask it about an area it has never seen, and it refuses, and says why. And a web service that answers the same questions, for any app or website. Its typical error on houses it has never seen is under twenty thousand pounds, and by the end you will know exactly what that means, and how far to trust it. Let's begin.

Every data project starts with two things: the data, and the tools to read it. Our folder is called house prices, and it arrives with exactly that. The terminal lists it: a data folder holding one file, homes dot csv, every house sold in the town of Millbrook over almost six years, and a file called pyproject dot toml, open in the editor. Its last block is a dependency group named notebook: four tools, each pinned to an exact version. pandas, for tables. NumPy, the fast arrays pandas is built on. matplotlib, for charts. And JupyterLab, the notebook we will work in. Back in the terminal, python three point fifteen, dash m, venv, makes the project its own Python in a folder called dot venv, and source activates it. Then one command reads the group and installs all four, into this project only: pip install, dash dash group, notebook. The side pane shows where they land: the virtual environment's site packages, nowhere else on the machine. The last two commands ask the tools themselves which versions arrived, and they match the pins exactly. That is the reason to pin. A later install could pick up a newer pandas that prints a table slightly differently, or changes a default, and a number in this course would quietly stop matching your screen. With the pins, every output you see here is one you can reproduce. Notice the project is not a Python package yet: no package folder, nothing to import. It is a folder with data and tools. It becomes a package in the last course, once there is code worth packaging.

Before the first cell, it is worth knowing what a notebook actually is, because it explains almost every surprise you will meet in one. A notebook is three programs and one file. Number one is the browser, running JupyterLab. It draws the cells, and when you run one, it sends that cell's code away. It does not run Python itself. Number two is the Jupyter server, a program on your machine. It passes the code along, carries the result back, and saves the notebook to disk. Number three is the kernel: one Python process, started when the notebook opens. It runs each cell it is sent, and here is the important part: it stays alive between cells. When cell one creates homes, the DataFrame stays in the kernel's memory, so every later cell can use it, without reading the file again. jupyter kernelspec list shows the kernel we are using, the python three kernel inside this project's own dot venv. Number four is the file. A notebook dot ipynb is plain JSON. On the right is cell one exactly as it was saved, printed by the lab: its cell type, its execution count, one, its output, the tuple one thousand four hundred and sixty, ten, and its source, line by line. So the file holds what you typed, and a record of what happened when it ran. The numbers in square brackets are that record: the order the kernel ran cells in. They are not line numbers, and they are not guaranteed to go top to bottom. Two sections from now, that difference produces a wrong answer, on purpose.

Here is the notebook, explore dot ipynb, with its first two cells. Cell one imports pandas under its usual short name, pd, then reads the sales with pd dot read csv. The path starts with dot dot, because a notebook runs from its own folder, notebooks, and the data sits one level up. The result is a DataFrame, which we name homes. The cell's last line is homes dot shape, and because it is the last line, the notebook prints its value under the cell: one thousand four hundred and sixty rows, ten columns. Cell two asks for homes dot head: the first five rows. The side pane shows what read csv did. At the top are the first lines of the file itself, plain text, values separated by commas. The first line is the header. Every other line became one row of the DataFrame, and the header became the column names: id, sold, agent, area, and on to price. Then pandas added something the file never had, the index, the bold zero, one, two down the left. It labels each row, and it is how pandas finds rows later. Now look harder at those five rows, because they already tell us about this data. Row one's sold date is written day first, with slashes, while the others are year first. Garage says N a N in two rows: Not a Number, pandas' mark for a missing value. And built is shown as nineteen sixty one point zero, a decimal, for a year. None of that is a mistake by pandas. It is the data, reporting itself honestly. The next section looks at how pandas stores it.

Cell three calls homes dot info, the first thing to run on any new data. It prints the DataFrame's structure: a range index from zero to one thousand four hundred and fifty nine, then one line per column, with how many values are present and the column's d type, its data type. The side pane draws what that means. A DataFrame is one index, shared by every row, plus a set of columns, and each column is its own object, a Series. A Series holds one data type, for every value in it. sqft is int sixty four, whole numbers. area is str, text. built and garage are float sixty four, and info explains why: garage has only one thousand and eleven values out of fourteen sixty. The rest are missing, and a missing value is stored as N a N, which is a float, so the whole column becomes floats. That is why a year printed as nineteen sixty one point zero. Now the surprise, highlighted in red. price is str: text, not a number. Cell four confirms it. Selecting one column with square brackets gives a Series, and its d type is a string type. Why? One estate agent typed some prices with a pound sign and commas, like pound two hundred and fifteen thousand. pandas reads a column one way only, and a column that holds even one value that is not a number must be text. So at the moment, we cannot even average a price. That is fine. The cleaning course fixes it properly, and finding it now, in the first minute, is exactly what info is for.

This section produces a wrong answer, on purpose, because every notebook user meets it eventually. Cell five keeps the big houses: homes over two thousand five hundred square feet, in a new DataFrame called big. Cell six asks how many there are, with len: one hundred and fifty four. Except that is not the answer to the question on screen. Look at the counts in the gutter. Cell five ran fifth, and cell six shows seven, not six. The side pane lays out what the kernel actually ran. Cell five first ran with an earlier version of its text: over two thousand. Cell six counted those homes, one hundred and fifty four. Then cell five was edited to two thousand five hundred, and never run again, so the kernel never saw the edit. Cell six ran once more, as count seven, and counted the same old big. The notebook now shows code that says one thing next to a result that comes from another. Nothing warned us. The fix is to stop trusting the order things happened to run in. In JupyterLab's Kernel menu, Restart Kernel and Run All Cells throws away everything in memory, and runs every cell top to bottom, once. The table at the bottom compares the two: as run, one hundred and fifty four, after a restart, thirty eight. Thirty eight is the right answer for two thousand five hundred square feet. The rule for the whole course: before you believe a result, or share a notebook, restart and run all. The counts should read one, two, three, in order, and from the next section on, they will.

After a restart and run all, the counts run in order, and len big now says thirty eight. One more idea finishes the setup, and it explains why the rest of this course writes code the way it does. Cell seven takes the sqft column out of pandas as a NumPy array, with to numpy. Its type is numpy dot n d array, its d type int sixty four, and it occupies eleven thousand, six hundred and eighty bytes: exactly fourteen sixty numbers times eight bytes each. The side pane shows why that matters. A NumPy array stores its numbers side by side, raw, all of one type. A Python list stores pointers, and each pointer leads to a separate integer object somewhere else in memory, with its own type and bookkeeping. Now the same job done both ways: convert every size from square feet to square metres, by dividing by ten point seven six four. Cell eight does it with a Python loop, one number at a time, and the percent timeit magic runs it many times and reports the average. Cell nine divides the whole array at once: sizes divided by ten point seven six four, no loop in sight. The timing table compares them. The exact times vary on every run and every machine, but the gap does not: the array is hundreds of times faster. The loop runs in Python, checking each object's type as it goes. The array runs one tight loop in compiled code, over numbers it already knows the type of. pandas columns are NumPy arrays underneath, so the habit for the whole course is: operate on whole columns, never loop over rows.

A DataFrame answers questions, but first you have to point at the part you mean. This course gets its own notebook, select dot ipynb, and cell one reads the sales again. Cell two picks columns: square brackets with a list of names gives a smaller DataFrame, here area, sqft and beds, and head of three shows its first rows. To reach a single value there are two tools, and the difference between them matters. dot loc works with labels. homes dot loc, two, area, means the row whose label is two, and the column named area: Riverside. dot iloc works with positions, counting from zero. homes dot iloc, two, three, means the third row and the fourth column, and that is also area: Riverside. The side pane lays the two side by side. Each row has a label, the index pandas added, and a position, where it sits right now. At the moment they are the same numbers, zero, one, two, because the rows are still in file order. That is why loc and iloc agree here. It is a coincidence, and the next sections end it. The habit worth building now: when you mean a particular house, use loc and its label. When you mean whatever happens to be in the third row at this moment, use iloc. Most of the time, in this course, you will mean a house.

Most questions about data start with which rows. Which homes are in Riverside? Cell five asks it in one comparison: homes area, equals equals, Riverside. pandas compares every row at once and gives back a Series of True and False, one per row, called a mask. The side pane lines them up: Hillcrest, false. Old Town, false. Riverside, true. A mask can be counted, because True counts as one: riverside dot sum is two hundred and forty six. And a mask can select: put it inside square brackets and only the True rows are kept. Cell seven combines two masks with an ampersand, which means and: in Riverside, and over two thousand square feet. Each condition sits in its own brackets, because the ampersand binds more tightly than the comparison. The result has twenty six rows and all ten columns. Notice there is no loop anywhere. Every comparison ran over the whole column in one go, which is the NumPy lesson from the last course, at work. But two hundred and forty six is not every sale in Riverside. The comparison is exact, character for character, and some rows spell the area with a space at the end. Those rows are silently left out. A filter that quietly misses rows is one of the most common wrong answers in data work, and we will find these in two sections' time.

Which are the biggest houses in Millbrook? Cell eight answers with nlargest: the five largest by sqft, keeping area, sqft and beds. The largest is in Riverside, three thousand eight hundred and thirty three square feet, and the list ends with a house from Old Town. Look at the labels down the left of that result: eleven eighty eight, six fifty, six ninety one, one seventy five, and one. Sorting moved the rows, and each row took its label with it. Now loc and iloc stop agreeing, and cell nine shows it. top dot loc, one, area, asks for the row labelled one: that is the old row one, the Old Town house, now sitting at the bottom of the list. top dot iloc one asks for whatever is second from the top right now: a house in Northgate. Same number, two different houses. The side pane marks both rows, with each row's current position next to its label. This is exactly why the index exists. After any amount of sorting and filtering, label one still means the same sale it meant when the file was read, so you can always find your way back to it. Use loc when you mean that house. Use iloc only when you mean a place in the current order, like the top row of a ranking.

New columns come from arithmetic on old ones, a whole column at a time. Cell ten works out each house's age: twenty twenty six minus built. One line, no loop, and the new column is simply assigned into homes under the name age. The tail of the result shows built and age side by side: built in nineteen fifty six, seventy years old. Built in two thousand and seven, nineteen. Notice the ages are decimals, seventy point zero, because built is a float column, and any year that is missing gives a missing age. A missing value in, a missing value out. pandas never invents an answer. So the next question is the obvious one: price per square foot, price divided by sqft. Cell eleven tries it, and it fails, with a type error: unsupported operand types for division, str and int. The side pane shows why. sqft is int sixty four, numbers. But price is str, text, the problem we found in the very first info. You cannot divide text by a number, and pandas refuses rather than guessing. This is the right behaviour. A tool that quietly turned pound two hundred and fifteen thousand into a number, or into nothing, would hand you a wrong average with no warning. So price per square foot waits. The cleaning course turns price into real numbers, and then this cell works.

Two sections ago a filter missed some Riverside sales. Cell twelve shows why. value counts lists every distinct value of area with how many times it appears, and there are seven, not five. Riverside appears twice: two hundred and forty six times as written, and twenty times with a space at the end. You cannot see that space in the output, which is exactly what makes it dangerous. And Old Town appears twice too, once with a small t. Cell thirteen fixes the spaces. The dot str accessor applies a string method to every value in a column, and strip removes spaces from both ends. Written back into homes, Riverside becomes one value with two hundred and sixty six sales, the side pane shows them merged. Old town with a small t is still there. It is a different slip, a matter of case, not spaces, and I am leaving it on purpose: in the course on joins it will make a real join fail, which is a far better way to learn to check for it. The last cell is about memory. A column of text stores a full string for every row. Converting it to the category type stores each distinct area once, plus a small code per row. The plot compares them: about eighty four thousand bytes as text, under two thousand as a category. Five areas repeated fourteen hundred times is exactly the shape category is made for.

The sold column is text, and dates as text cannot be sorted by time or grouped by month. Cell fifteen does the obvious thing, pd dot to datetime, and it fails. pandas looked at the first value, saw year, month, day, assumed every row was written that way, and then met eight, slash, oh one, twenty twenty one, written by a different agent. The error even suggests passing format mixed and letting pandas guess each row. Do not. Eight oh one could be the eighth of January or the first of August, and a guess that is wrong for some rows produces dates that look fine and are not. We know the two formats, so cell sixteen says so. It parses the column twice. Once as year, month, day, and once as day, month, year, each time with errors equals coerce, which turns anything that does not match into NaT, Not a Time, instead of failing. The side pane follows two real rows through it. Each format parses its own rows and leaves the other's as NaT, and fillna fills the gaps of the first with the second. The check that matters is underneath: zero missing dates, and a real datetime type. Now the dates behave like dates. Cell seventeen takes the year of every sale with dot dt dot year, and counts them. The chart shows a steady market, about two hundred and fifty sales a year, with twenty twenty six lower only because the data stops in September.

One last rule about selecting, and it is about changing data rather than reading it. Somewhere in this data is a house with twelve bedrooms, and it is a typo. Fixing it properly is a job for the cleaning course, so here we practise on a copy called demo. Cell eighteen tries the natural looking line: select the rows where beds is twelve, then their beds column, and set it to two. pandas warns, with a chained assignment error, and the maximum is still twelve. Nothing changed. The side pane shows why. demo, square brackets, mask, is a new object, and in pandas three it always behaves as a copy. That rule is called Copy-on-Write. Setting beds on it changes the copy, which is then thrown away, so the original never sees the edit. Older versions of pandas sometimes changed the original and sometimes did not, and printed a vague warning either way. pandas three made it one simple rule: a chain like this never changes the original. Cell nineteen does it in one step: demo dot loc, with the row condition and the column name inside the same brackets, equals two. Now the maximum is six. So whenever you change values in a DataFrame, use loc with both the rows and the column at once. That is how the cleaning course will fix this typo for real.

Every finding later in this course depends on the rows being right, so this course goes through the data fault by fault, in a new notebook, clean dot ipynb. The first question for any dataset is what is missing. Cell one reads the raw sales and calls homes dot isna dot sum. isna gives True wherever a value is missing, and sum counts the Trues, column by column. Eight columns are complete. Two are not: built is missing thirteen times, and garage four hundred and forty nine times. Cell two swaps sum for mean, which turns the counts into shares: under one percent of build years, but almost thirty one percent of garages. Nearly a third of a column is empty. The side pane shows where a gap comes from. In the file it is simply nothing between two commas, and read csv turns nothing into N a N. N a N is a floating point value, which is why both of these whole number columns came out as floats in the first course. So now we know how much is missing. The harder question, and the next section, is what each gap actually means, because the right fix depends entirely on that, and getting it wrong quietly changes every average that follows.

Why would a third of the garages be missing? Cell three counts the values of garage with dropna false, so the gaps are counted too. One garage, five hundred and seventy four houses. Two, three hundred and seventy five. Three, sixty two. And N a N, four hundred and forty nine. Look at what is not in that list: zero. Not one house in the whole export is recorded as having no garage. That is the evidence. The agents left the field empty when there was no garage, so here, empty means zero. Cell four fills those gaps with zero and makes the column whole numbers again, and checks what is still missing: only built, thirteen times. Built gets a different decision, shown in the side pane. These are old houses whose build year nobody knows. We could fill them with the average year, but that would plant thirteen made-up facts in the data, and an old cottage would suddenly look like it was built in the nineteen seventies. So built stays missing, and we will deal with it openly when a model needs a value. That is the rule for every gap: fill it only when the data itself tells you what it means, and otherwise leave it missing, and say so. A filled gap you cannot justify is worse than a gap.

Now the problem we have known about since the first info: price is text. Before fixing it, find out exactly which values are the trouble. Cell five uses pd dot to numeric with errors equals coerce. Every price that is a plain number converts, and anything else becomes N a N, so the N a Ns point straight at the problem rows. Selecting them shows the pattern: pound sign, a comma for thousands, and every one of them from the same agent, Bloom. Cell six counts them: forty five. Forty five rows out of fourteen hundred and sixty turned a whole column into text. Now that the pattern is known, the fix is exact rather than hopeful. Cell seven removes the pound sign, removes the commas, and converts. The side pane follows one real price through it: pound one hundred and ninety thousand eight hundred, then without the pound sign, then without the comma, and finally a number. This time to numeric is called without errors equals coerce, and that matters. If any value still could not be converted, the cell would fail loudly, instead of quietly turning it into a gap. The result is int sixty four, and the question we could not ask until now finally has an answer: the median price in Millbrook is two hundred and fifty one thousand, four hundred pounds.

Some faults are not visible in any single value. A house of a hundred and forty four square feet looks odd, but not impossible. It only becomes impossible next to its four bedrooms. Cell eight parses the dates, using last course's two formats, and then works out square feet per bedroom. The typical house has about four hundred and eighty five square feet per bedroom. The minimum is thirty. Cell nine lists the houses under two hundred, and they share a pattern: all from Keyline, all in the spring of twenty twenty three. That is not how real houses cluster. It is how a data entry mistake clusters. Keyline recorded those sales in square metres. Cell ten defines the batch the way the agent would describe it, by agent and by dates, rather than by the suspicious numbers. Twenty sales, all twenty of them under two hundred. Then it checks what the batch definition leaves out: one more house under two hundred elsewhere. Remember that one, it is a different fault, and the next section but one finds it. Cell eleven converts the batch to square feet, multiplying by ten point seven six four, and the minimum jumps from thirty to ninety one. Fixing by the batch's description, not by the symptom, matters: a rule like anything under two hundred gets fixed would have quietly altered a house that was wrong for a completely different reason.

A duplicate row is one sale counted twice, and it quietly inflates every count and tilts every average towards the houses that happen to be repeated. Cell twelve asks pandas: homes dot duplicated dot sum. duplicated marks a row True when an identical row has already appeared above it, so the sum counts the second copies: six. Cell thirteen shows them in pairs, using keep equals False, which marks both copies so you can see them side by side. Same id, same date, same area, same price, every column equal. Not two houses that happen to sell for the same price on the same day, which would be possible, but one sale with one id, entered twice. That shared id is what makes this safe to call a duplicate. Cell fourteen removes them with drop duplicates, which keeps the first copy of each, and the shape drops from fourteen hundred and sixty rows to fourteen hundred and fifty four. Notice that duplicated compares whole rows. Two rows with the same id but a different price would not be caught by this, and in real data you would then have to decide which record is right. Here, every duplicate is an exact copy, so the decision is simple, and we have it in writing.

describe gives the shape of a column in eight numbers, and cell fifteen asks for beds and price. Two numbers stand out. Somebody has twelve bedrooms, and somebody paid ten thousand pounds for a house. A common way to flag unusual values is the interquartile range. Take the middle half of the prices, from the twenty fifth percentile to the seventy fifth. Then put a fence one and a half times that width beyond each end. Cell sixteen computes the fences: about seventy six thousand pounds below, about four hundred and thirty nine thousand above. One price falls below the low fence. Thirty six fall above the high one. Here is the part that matters: a fence finds rows to look at. It does not find errors. Cell seventeen looks. The twelve bedroom house has one thousand and ninety six square feet, which is the house we met two sections ago, and a two with a stray one in front. The ten thousand pound sale is a family transfer, not a market sale, so it does not belong in data about market prices. And the thirty six expensive houses? They are simply big houses in good areas, which is exactly what we want a model to learn about. Cell eighteen makes exactly two changes: fix the typo with loc, and drop the transfer. Fourteen hundred and fifty three sales remain.

Before turning this notebook into one reusable function, it is worth naming what we were aiming for, because it has a name: tidy data. Tidy data follows three rules, and this export broke all three. Rule one: each variable is one column, of one type. Price mixed numbers and text, forty five rows like pound one hundred and ninety thousand eight hundred, and sold mixed two date formats. Rule two: each observation, here each sale, is exactly one row. Six sales were entered twice, and one row was not a sale at all, the ten thousand pound transfer. Rule three is the subtle one: each value means one thing. In sqft, twenty values meant square metres. In garage, empty meant zero. In area, Riverside with a trailing space meant Riverside. The ledger on the right lists every fix with the number of rows it touched, and at the bottom, the effect of the whole thing: fourteen hundred and sixty rows in, fourteen hundred and fifty three out. Underneath it is the same sale, before and after: day-first date with slashes in the raw file, ISO date and a zero for the garage in the clean one. None of these fixes was clever. What made them right was that each one was found with a check, explained by the data, and recorded. That is what makes the clean file trustworthy.

Fixes spread across a dozen cells are hard to repeat. If next month's export arrives, you would have to rerun them all in the right order and hope. So cell nineteen gathers every rule into one function, clean, which takes the raw table and returns a tidy one. Inside, it parses the dates in both formats, then builds the result as one chain. assign replaces six columns at once: sold, area stripped of spaces, garage filled with zero, price converted to numbers, sqft fixed for the square metre batch, and the bedroom typo corrected. Then drop duplicates, then query keeps only market sales. The side pane draws the chain: raw in at the top, tidy out at the bottom. Cell twenty runs it on a fresh read of the raw file, and then asserts what must be true of the result: price is whole numbers, every sale has a date, there are no duplicates, and no house has more than six bedrooms. An assert does nothing when it holds and stops the notebook with an error when it does not. They are the notebook checking its own work. The answer: fourteen hundred and sixty rows in, fourteen hundred and fifty three out, exactly what the cell-by-cell fixes produced. Cell twenty one saves the result as homes clean dot csv, new in the explorer. From the next course on, every notebook starts from that file, not the raw export.

With clean data, the questions can finally be about houses. This course works in shape dot ipynb, and cell one reads the clean file from the last course, asking pandas to parse sold as dates: one thousand four hundred and fifty three sales. Which area costs most? Cell two answers in one line: homes, group by area, the price column, median, sorted. The side pane shows what that line does, in three steps with a famous name: split, apply, combine. Split divides the rows into one group per area. Apply runs the median on each group's prices separately. Combine collects the answers into one Series, labelled by area. Eastfield is cheapest, at about two hundred and twenty eight thousand pounds. Riverside is the most expensive, at about two hundred and ninety three thousand. The code underneath is the same split, apply, combine written as a loop and a dictionary. groupby does it in one call, and fast, because each group is still a NumPy array underneath. But count the groups. There are six, not five. Old town, with the small t, is still its own area, with its own median. groupby takes the spelling exactly as written, just as the double equals did in the select course. Hold on to that. In three sections it becomes a real problem.

One statistic per group is rarely enough. Cell three asks for three at once with agg and named aggregations. First it adds a column we could not compute two courses ago: price per square foot, price divided by sqft. It works now, because cleaning turned price into numbers. Then agg takes keyword arguments, and each one is a new column name, equals, a pair: which column to use, and which function to apply. sales is the size of each group's price column, in other words the number of sales. median price is the median of price. median per sqft is the median of the new column. The result is one tidy table, one row per area, with three named columns, rounded. The side pane spells out the pattern, and charts price per square foot by area. Riverside leads again, at two hundred and sixteen pounds per square foot, and Eastfield is lowest, at a hundred and sixty six. That matters, because it rules out a dull explanation. Riverside is not more expensive only because its houses happen to be bigger. Each square foot there costs more. Per square foot is often the fairer comparison between areas, and it is one we will come back to when we build features for a model.

groupby with one key gives a list. Group by two keys, and the natural shape is a grid. Cell four builds one with pivot table: areas down the side, bedroom counts across the top, and in each cell the median price of the sales that fall in it. The side pane names the four arguments. index decides the rows. columns decides the columns. values is what fills the cells, and aggfunc says how each cell sums up its sales, here the median. round minus three rounds to the nearest thousand pounds, so the grid is readable. Read along a row and prices climb with bedrooms, as you would expect. Read down a column and the areas order themselves much as they did by median. The plot picks two rows: Riverside and Eastfield. With one bedroom, Riverside is about seventy thousand pounds dearer. The gap holds at every size up to five bedrooms. The six bedroom column is left off the plot on purpose: a six bedroom house is rare, so each of those cells stands on only a handful of sales, and a median of a handful is fragile. A pivot table shows you a number in every cell whether it stands on two sales or two hundred, so always ask how many. That question, how sure we can be, gets a whole course of its own.

Some things that set a price are not in the sales file at all: how good the local school is, how far the centre is, whether the area floods. A second file, areas dot csv, now in the data folder, holds them, one row per area, and cell five shows all five. Joining them onto the sales is a merge on the area column. Cell six does it carefully. how equals left keeps every sale whether or not it finds a match. validate equals many to one checks that each area appears only once in the areas table, so a sale can never be silently duplicated. And indicator equals True adds a column saying where each row found its match. The count is the point: one thousand four hundred and thirty three sales matched both sides. Twenty matched nothing. Cell seven lists the areas behind those twenty, and there it is: Old town, small t. The side pane shows the keys. Old Town with a capital T finds its row in areas. Old town with a small one finds nothing, because a merge compares text exactly, like everything else. This is why I left it unfixed two courses ago: a join is where a spelling slip really bites. Cell nine fixes it with str dot title, merges for real, and the shape confirms it: fourteen hundred and fifty three sales, every one now carrying fourteen columns.

Before moving on, it is worth seeing exactly what the different kinds of join would have done with that spelling slip, because the default is the dangerous one. On the left, the two sides: the sales, whose area column still includes Old town with a small t, and the areas table, with its five spellings. In the middle, the four joins, each with its real row count, from one line in the notebook. An inner join keeps only rows whose key is found on both sides: fourteen hundred and thirty three. A left join keeps every row from the left, and fills the areas' columns with N a N where nothing matched: fourteen hundred and fifty three. A right join keeps every row from the right, here every area, so it loses the same twenty sales. And outer keeps everything from both sides. Here it equals the left join, because every area has at least one sale. Now the lesson. pandas' merge is an inner join unless you ask otherwise. Run the obvious line, get no error, no warning, and twenty sales have simply gone, only visible if you happened to compare row counts. So the habits on the right are worth keeping: start with a left join, ask for the indicator, validate the relationship, and compare the row count before and after every join you ever write.

Prices are not fixed in time, and a model that ignores when a house sold will blame the house for the market. Because sold is a real datetime column, pandas can group by time. Cell ten sets sold as the index, and resample quarterly, Q S for quarter start, takes the median price in each quarter. Resample is groupby for time: it makes the time buckets for you, even quarters with no sales. Quarterly medians jump about, because each quarter holds only about sixty sales, and which houses happen to sell matters. So the same cell adds a rolling mean over four quarters. Each value is the average of the last four, which smooths the noise and shows the direction. The first three are N a N, because there are not yet four quarters to average. The plot shows both. The blue line jitters, the orange one climbs steadily. Cell eleven measures that climb, from the first rolling value to the last: up twenty three point eight percent across the period. That is a real feature of this market, and an important one. A house sold in twenty twenty one and an identical one sold in twenty twenty six did not sell for the same price. When we come to build a model, the date of sale has to be one of its inputs.

The last tool in this course is about shape itself. Cell twelve builds a pivot of median price by year and area: six years down, five areas across. That is wide data, one column per area. It reads beautifully as a table, and you can compare areas along each row. But a column per area is awkward to compute with. Add a sixth area and the table grows a column. Ask for the median across all areas and years, and you have to pull numbers from five columns at once. Cell thirteen converts it with melt. The year becomes a column called sold, each area name moves into a column called area, and each price into a column called median. Cell fourteen compares shapes: six rows by five columns wide, and thirty rows by three columns long. Exactly the same thirty numbers, arranged two ways. The side pane shows both, with the first few rows of each. Long data is what pandas, plotting libraries and models want: one observation per row, every variable a column. That is just the tidy rule from the cleaning course again. Wide is how people like to read. So keep your data long while you work, and pivot it wide at the very end, when a human needs to read it. melt takes you from wide to long, and pivot takes you back.

Numbers in a table tell you a lot. A picture tells you what to ask next. This course's notebook, see dot ipynb, starts by reading the clean sales, fixing the area spelling and joining the area facts, the last course in three lines. Then one question: what do prices look like as a whole? The first cell gives three numbers. The mean is about two hundred and sixty two thousand five hundred pounds, the median two hundred and fifty one thousand four hundred, and a third number, skew, is zero point eight two. Cell two draws the histogram: prices cut into bins twenty five thousand pounds wide, each bar the number of sales in its bin. The notebook draws the figure matplotlib made, from exactly the numbers it plotted. The shape explains the three numbers. Most sales pile up in the middle, near the median, and then a long tail stretches out to the right: a few expensive houses, far from the rest. Those few pull the mean towards them, which is why it sits eleven thousand pounds above the median. That is what a positive skew means: a longer tail on the right. For prices, incomes and anything else with a long right tail, the median is the better summary of a typical value. It is the price of the house in the middle, and a single mansion cannot move it.

There is another way to look at the same prices, and it matters a great deal later. Cell three takes the base ten logarithm of every price and draws its histogram. The long tail has gone. The shape is almost a symmetric bell. Cell four confirms it in numbers: the skew drops from zero point eight two to minus zero point zero five, and the mean and median of the logged prices are almost identical. Why would taking a logarithm do that? The side pane shows the reason. On a log scale, equal ratios become equal distances. Two hundred thousand to two hundred and twenty thousand is a ten percent rise, and so is five hundred thousand to five hundred and fifty thousand. In pounds the second step is two and a half times bigger. In log ten, both steps are exactly the same, zero point zero four one. And prices really do behave in percentages. A good garage might add a few percent to any house, not a fixed number of pounds, and the market rose by a percentage too. Things that combine by multiplying produce a right skewed distribution, and the logarithm turns multiplying back into adding. Keep this in mind for the modelling course. A model fitted on log prices makes errors in percentages, and for houses, that is almost always the error you care about.

One variable at a time only goes so far. The interesting questions are about how two variables move together. Cell five draws a scatter plot: every sale is one dot, placed by its size across and its price up. Fourteen hundred and fifty three dots, small and partly transparent, so that dense areas show up darker. The pattern is obvious at a glance: bigger houses cost more, and the dots climb from bottom left to top right. Cell six puts a number on it with the correlation, r, between sqft and price: zero point eight two eight. The side pane gives the scale. Plus one would be every dot on a rising straight line. Zero would mean no straight line link at all. Minus one, a perfect falling line. Zero point eight three is strong. But the picture shows two things the single number cannot. First, the cloud widens to the right. Big houses vary more in price, in pounds, which is the percentage effect from the last section again. Second, look at what is not there: no cluster of houses far below everything else. Before cleaning, the twenty sales recorded in square metres would have sat in a strange group at the far left. The scatter is also a check that the cleaning course did its job.

When we compared areas in the last course we used one number each, the median. A median hides how spread out a group is, so this section draws the spread too. Cell seven computes three quantiles per area: the twenty fifth percentile, the median, and the seventy fifth, sorted by the median and rounded to the nearest thousand. Between the twenty fifth and seventy fifth percentile lies the middle half of each area's sales. Cell eight draws it: a bar for each median, and a black line from the twenty fifth to the seventy fifth percentile, drawn with vlines. The table on the right holds the same numbers. Look at how much the lines overlap. Riverside is clearly the dearest area, and Eastfield the cheapest, yet the middle halves still overlap. The dearer quarter of Eastfield sales starts at about two hundred and sixty six thousand pounds, which is more than the cheaper quarter of Riverside sales, from about two hundred and forty five thousand. Plenty of Eastfield houses cost more than plenty of Riverside houses. That is what the area medians alone hide. Area matters, but it is far from the whole story, and any model that predicted a house's price from its area alone would be wrong by tens of thousands of pounds, for a lot of houses.

With several numeric columns, you can ask for every correlation at once. Cell nine takes eight of them, price, size, bedrooms, year built, garage, condition, school rating and distance to the centre, and calls corr. The result is a matrix: every column against every other, with ones down the diagonal, where each column meets itself. It is a lot to read, so cell ten keeps just the column that matters most to us, correlation with price, and sorts it. The side pane draws it as bars. Size leads, at zero point eight three. Bedrooms follow at zero point six seven, but bedrooms and size are themselves correlated at zero point eight, so they largely carry the same information twice. School rating, zero point two eight. Distance to the centre is negative, minus zero point two: further out, cheaper. And then some surprises. Condition, zero point one. Garage, zero point zero nine, almost nothing, even though garages surely add value. And built, zero point one three, as if newer houses cost more. Remember what r measures: a straight line link between two columns, one pair at a time, ignoring everything else. A garage's effect can be hidden by everything else that varies at the same time. And built's link may not be built's at all. The next course takes both of these apart properly.

A chart makes a claim, and the same numbers can make a true one or a false one. Cell eleven takes two medians, Eastfield and Riverside, and draws them as bars from zero, on the right. Cell twelve, in the notebook, draws exactly the same two numbers, with one change: the vertical axis starts at two hundred and twenty thousand pounds. The next cell divides one by the other, and the side pane shows the true answer: Riverside's median is one point two eight times Eastfield's, twenty eight percent higher. The first chart shows that honestly. The second chart's bars make Riverside look about nine times dearer, because the bars now start at two hundred and twenty thousand, and most of each bar has been cut off. Nothing on the second chart is false. The axis is labelled, and the numbers are right. But a bar's length is its claim, and the lengths are wrong. The rules on the right are short. Bars start at zero, because the reader compares their lengths. Lines and scatter plots may zoom in, because the reader compares positions, and zooming is often the only way to see a trend. And every axis needs a label and a unit. This closes the exploring half of the course. We have clean data, and we can describe, group, join and draw it. Next comes the harder question: how sure can we be about any of it?

Everything so far has described the sales we have. This course asks how far those descriptions can be trusted, in a new notebook, stats dot ipynb. It starts with the two kinds of summary every dataset needs: where the middle is, and how spread out the values are. Cell one gives the mean, the median and the standard deviation of price: about two hundred and sixty two thousand, two hundred and fifty one thousand, and seventy three thousand pounds. Cell two gives another measure of spread, the interquartile range, the width of the middle half: about ninety one thousand pounds. Then cell three runs an experiment. It adds one imaginary sale, a five million pound mansion, to the fourteen hundred and fifty three real ones, and summarises again. The side pane shows the damage. One sale out of fourteen hundred and fifty four moves the mean by more than three thousand pounds, and nearly doubles the standard deviation. The median moves by fifty pounds. Statisticians call the median and the interquartile range robust: they describe the typical sale, and a single extreme value cannot drag them around. Real house price data always has a few extraordinary sales, so for prices, quote the median and the interquartile range. Use the mean and standard deviation when you know the values are well behaved, and when a model needs them.

We have fourteen hundred and fifty three sales, but they are only the sales that happened. Any dataset is a sample of a bigger world, and a sample gives an answer that is a little off. How far off? This section finds out by experiment, using the data itself as the whole world. Cell four draws one random sample of a hundred sales. random state equals one fixes the draw, so it replays exactly. Its median is two hundred and thirty nine thousand, four hundred and fifty pounds, about twelve thousand pounds below the median of every sale. Is that bad luck, or normal? Cell five draws a thousand different samples of a hundred, each with its own random state, and keeps each one's median. describe summarises those thousand medians. They centre on the true median, two hundred and fifty one thousand four hundred. But they spread out, with a standard deviation of about seven thousand eight hundred pounds, from about two hundred and thirty one thousand at the lowest to two hundred and eighty four thousand at the highest. Cell six draws their histogram. That bell is called a sampling distribution: every answer one sample of a hundred could have given you. Our first sample, twelve thousand pounds off, was a bit unlucky but entirely normal. The catch is that in real life you only ever get one sample. The next section shows how to estimate that spread from the one sample you have.

The bootstrap is one of the most useful ideas in statistics, and it fits on one screen. The question: Riverside has two hundred and sixty six sales, with a median of two hundred and ninety three thousand and fifty pounds. How sure can we be of that number, with no other sample to compare it with? Step one, start from the one sample we have. Step two, draw two hundred and sixty six sales from it, with replacement: each draw can pick any sale, including one already picked. So the new sample has some sales twice and some not at all, and its median comes out a little different. That new sample is a plausible alternative version of Riverside's sales. Step three, repeat that two thousand times, keeping each median. Their histogram, on the right, is the bootstrap's estimate of the sampling distribution from the last section, made from one sample alone. Step four, keep the middle ninety five percent: cut off the lowest two and a half percent and the highest two and a half percent. What remains is a ninety five percent confidence interval: from two hundred and seventy eight thousand one hundred to three hundred and one thousand four hundred pounds. The table checks the hand made version against SciPy's bootstrap function, with its own seed. They agree to within a few hundred pounds, which is exactly as close as two different sets of random draws should.

Here is the bootstrap as it really runs in the notebook. Cell seven selects Riverside's prices: two hundred and sixty six sales, median two hundred and ninety three thousand and fifty pounds. Cell eight is the whole bootstrap in one expression: two thousand times, sample the prices with replacement, at the same size, with a fixed random state each time, and keep the median. Then the two point five and ninety seven point five percent quantiles of those medians give the interval. Cell ten does the same with SciPy, which this section adds to the project. pyproject dot toml gains one pinned line, scipy, and the notebook group is installed again. stats dot bootstrap takes the data, the statistic, the number of resamples, the method, and a seed, and it returns the same interval within a few hundred pounds. The side pane draws the bootstrap medians with the two cut-off points marked. So the honest way to report Riverside's typical price is not a single number. It is: about two hundred and ninety three thousand pounds, likely between two hundred and seventy eight and three hundred and one thousand. That interval says how much the answer could move with a different set of sales. It shrinks as the sample grows, and for a small area with twenty sales it would be very wide. A number without its interval looks more certain than it is.

Correlation said garages barely relate to price. Let us ask the question directly. Cell eleven compares the median price of houses with a garage against those without: houses with a garage sell for thirteen thousand and fifty pounds more. But some gap would appear by luck even if garages meant nothing at all. How do we tell a real gap from a lucky one? The permutation test answers by simulating a world where garages do not matter. The side pane gives the idea. Keep every price exactly where it is, but shuffle which houses are marked as having a garage. In that shuffled world any gap is pure luck. Measure the median gap again. Do that five thousand times, and count how often luck alone produced a gap at least as big as the real one. Cell twelve writes this as a small function, shuffled differences, with a seeded random generator so it replays. The answer is zero point zero zero three six: only thirty six shuffles in ten thousand reach thirteen thousand pounds. Cell thirteen draws all five thousand shuffled gaps, with the real one marked in red, far out in the right tail. So a gap this large would be very unusual if garages did not matter. That fraction has a name: the p value. The next section is about what it does and does not mean.

A p value of zero point zero zero three six is easy to misread, so this section takes it apart. First, what it says: if garages made no difference, a gap this big would turn up by luck in fewer than four tries in a thousand. So the gap is very probably real. What it does not say is how big the effect is. Cell fourteen measures that directly: the gap is five point two percent of the median price. Whether five percent matters depends on you, not on the p value. Nor does it say what causes the gap. Houses with garages might also be bigger, or in better areas. Now the second cell, which is the important one. It asks exactly the same question of a random forty sales. The gap is still there, eighteen thousand pounds, but the p value is zero point five. Half of all shuffles do as well. With forty sales, there is no evidence at all. And this is where people go wrong: no evidence of an effect is not evidence of no effect. The garage effect in Millbrook did not change. The data was simply too small to see it. The table puts the two side by side: same question, same kind of gap, opposite conclusions, and the only difference is the amount of data. Always report the size of an effect and its interval, and treat a p value as one piece of evidence, never as the answer.

Two courses ago, correlation suggested that newer houses cost more: built and price correlated at zero point one three. Cell sixteen repeats it. Is it true that a newer house is worth more, all else equal? Cell seventeen looks at where the new houses are. The median year built differs hugely between areas: Old Town's houses date from the nineteen thirties, Riverside's from the two thousands. And Riverside, from earlier courses, is the dearest area. So there is another explanation. Area could be driving both: dear areas happen to have newer houses, and dear areas have higher prices. The side pane draws that: area points at built, and area points at price, with no arrow between built and price at all. A variable like area, which drives both of the things you are comparing, is called a confounder. Cell eighteen tests it by holding area fixed. Inside each area separately, the correlation between built and price is close to zero: point zero six, minus point zero nine, point zero five. Within an area, a newer house is not worth more. The overall zero point one three was the area talking all along. The general lesson: a correlation between two columns can be produced by a third. Before believing that one thing affects another, ask what else differs between the houses, and compare like with like. In the modelling course, putting area into the model alongside built does exactly that.

Time to answer the question the whole course is about: what is this house worth? Answering it with a model starts by deciding exactly what the model sees. This notebook, model dot ipynb, will carry us through three courses, and this section adds scikit learn, the standard Python library for machine learning, pinned like everything else in pyproject dot toml. Cell one reads the clean sales and adds one column. A model cannot use a date directly, so months counts the months since January twenty twenty one: zero for a sale that month, sixty eight for September twenty twenty six. That lets the model learn the rising market we measured in the shape course. Cell two makes the split every machine learning problem starts with. y is the target, the column to predict: price. X holds the features, the columns the model may use: size, bedrooms, year built, garages, condition, area and months. Seven features, fourteen hundred and fifty three rows. Cell three shows the first rows of X. The side pane also lists what was left out, on purpose. id is a label, not a property of a house. agent says who sold it, not what it is. And price is not a feature, because it is the answer. That last one sounds obvious. In the leakage section we will see how easily the answer can sneak in anyway.

A model that is scored on the same houses it learned from will always look better than it really is. It can partly memorise them. So before any model exists, we set some houses aside. Cell four uses train test split. It shuffles the rows, with random state fixed so the shuffle replays, and puts twenty percent aside as a test set. One thousand one hundred and sixty two sales to train on, two hundred and ninety one to test with. The side pane shows the plan. The model learns only from the training rows. The test rows stay locked away until the very end, when they act as houses the model has never seen, like the next one that comes onto the market. Cell five checks that the split is fair: the median price is about two hundred and fifty three thousand pounds in the training set, and two hundred and forty seven thousand in the test set. Close, as it should be with a random shuffle, and not identical, also as it should be. One honest note. A random split mixes old and new sales together. If the real job were forecasting next year's prices, we would split by time instead, training on the past and testing on the future. Here the job is valuing a house today, given recent sales, so a random split is a fair exam.

This is the most important mistake in machine learning, and it looks like success. On the left is a feature that seems reasonable. In the shape course we found that price per square foot differs by area, so why not give the model price per square foot? The cell builds two features: the log of size, and the log of price per square foot. Look at line four. Price per square foot is price divided by size. It is built from y, the very thing we are trying to predict. The table shows what happens on the test set. R squared measures how much of the variation in price a model explains, where one point zero is perfect. Size alone explains zero point seven one. Add price per square foot, and the score is exactly one point zero. Perfect. And completely useless. Below, a house we actually want to value: we know its size, fifteen hundred square feet. Its price per square foot? To know that, we would need its price, which is what we are trying to find. That is leakage: information about the answer getting into the features. It always looks like brilliant performance, and it always fails the moment the model meets a real house. The table at the bottom lists quieter versions of the same mistake, and the question that catches all of them: would I know this value at the moment I need the prediction?

Models do arithmetic, so every feature has to be a number. Size and bedrooms already are. Area is text. Cell eight converts it with a one hot encoder, fitted on the training rows. get feature names out shows what it learned: five new columns, area Eastfield, area Hillcrest, area Northgate, area Old Town and area Riverside. Cell nine applies it to three real rows. An Old Town house gets a one in the Old Town column and zeros everywhere else. A Hillcrest house gets its one in the Hillcrest column. That is all one hot means: one column per category, and a single one, hot, in the right place. Why not simply number the areas, one to five? The side pane shows the problem. Numbers have an order and a size. If Eastfield were one and Riverside five, a model would read Riverside as five times Eastfield, and Hillcrest as somewhere between one and three. None of that means anything for areas. One hot columns carry no order and no distance. Each one only asks: is this house in this area, yes or no? And because the encoder is fitted on the training rows, an area it has never seen would be flagged, rather than silently given a meaning.

Features arrive on very different scales. Size runs to thousands of square feet, garages from zero to three, and year built sits around nineteen seventy. Many models work better, and their coefficients are easier to compare, when every number is on the same scale. A standard scaler does it. Cell ten fits one on the training rows only, for size and year built, and shows what it learned: a mean size of about fourteen hundred and thirteen square feet with a standard deviation of four hundred and forty seven, and a mean year of nineteen seventy two, with a standard deviation of twenty eight and a half. Scaling then subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation, so a value becomes: how many standard deviations from the training average. Cell eleven applies that same scaler to the test rows, and summarises the result. The means are close to zero, but not exactly: zero point zero three for size, minus zero point one one for built. The standard deviations are close to one, but not exactly. And that is correct. The scaler only knows the training rows, so the test rows are measured on the training scale, as a brand new house would be. If you fitted the scaler on all the rows, the test numbers would come out perfect, because test information had leaked into the scaler. Fit on train, apply to both.

Every preparation step so far has to be fitted on the training rows and then applied, in the same way, to any other rows. Doing that by hand, step by step, is exactly where leakage creeps in. scikit learn solves it with pipelines. Cell twelve builds the whole preparation as one object, called prepare. A column transformer sends different columns to different steps. The six number columns go through a small pipeline of their own: first a simple imputer, which fills the missing year built values with the median, the decision the cleaning course deferred until a model needed it. Then the standard scaler. The area column goes to the one hot encoder. Displaying prepare prints the whole structure. Cell thirteen fits it on the training rows and transforms them in one call. The result has eleven hundred and sixty two rows and eleven columns: six scaled numbers, and five area columns, with the names to prove it. The side pane draws the structure. The real value of this object is what comes next. In the modelling course, the model goes on the end of this pipeline. Then a single fit learns every step, imputing, scaling, encoding and modelling, from the training rows alone, and a single predict applies all of them to a new house. No step can peek at the test set, because no step ever sees it during fitting.

Before building a real model, build a terrible one on purpose. A baseline tells you what knowing nothing scores, so that every later model can be judged against it. Cell fourteen makes the simplest guess possible: for every house in the test set, predict the median price of the training set, the same number every time, whatever the house. Then it scores the guess with the mean absolute error, which the side pane spells out. For each test house, take the difference between the actual price and the predicted one, ignore whether it is above or below, and average those differences. The result is in pounds, which makes it easy to understand: on average, the guess is off by this much. For the baseline it is fifty nine thousand five hundred and eighty one pounds. That is the number to beat. A model that cannot do better than fifty nine and a half thousand pounds of typical error has learned nothing about houses at all, however clever it looks. It sounds too obvious to bother with. In practice, a surprising number of impressive looking models, published or deployed, turn out to barely beat a baseline like this one, because nobody computed it. So always compute it first. It takes one line, and it keeps every later number honest.

The first real model uses the strongest single feature we found: size. Cell fifteen fits a linear regression of price on sqft, using the training rows only. Fitting means choosing the straight line through the data that is, in a sense we will look at next, closest to all the points. The model learns two numbers. The intercept, about seventy seven thousand pounds, is where the line meets zero square feet. And the slope, one hundred and thirty one pounds and ten pence, is the price of each extra square foot. Then the cell predicts the test houses and scores them: a mean absolute error of thirty two thousand, six hundred and forty eight pounds. Size alone has cut the baseline's error nearly in half. The next cell draws it, on the right: the test houses as a scatter, and the fitted line in red, running through the middle of the cloud. Notice what the line cannot do. Two houses of the same size, one in Riverside and one in Eastfield, get exactly the same prediction, because the model has only ever been shown size. Every point above the line is a house worth more than its size suggests, and every point below, less. The distance from each point to the line is that house's error. How does fit choose the line? That is the next section.

Out of every possible straight line, how does linear regression pick one? The answer is called least squares, and it is three steps. Step one: any line makes an error for each house, the actual price minus what the line says. The table shows four real test houses. One sold for thirty eight thousand pounds more than the line predicted, another for fifty three thousand less. Step two: square every error, take the mean, and then the square root, to get back to pounds. That is the root mean squared error. Squaring does two things. A miss above can no longer cancel a miss below, and a big miss counts far more than a small one: twice the error, four times the penalty. Step three: the best line is the one with the smallest root mean squared error. The plot shows that search done by brute force. The notebook tried every slope from one hundred to one hundred and eighty pounds per square foot, with its best intercept, and measured the error of each. The curve falls, reaches a minimum, and rises again. The bottom of the curve sits at one hundred and thirty one pounds, exactly the slope linear regression found in the last section. The difference is that linear regression does not try slopes. It solves for the bottom directly, with a formula, which is why fitting is instant even with many features.

Now the model gets every feature. Cell nineteen builds a pipeline: the missing build years filled with the median, area one hot encoded with Eastfield dropped as the reference, and a linear regression on the end. One fit on the training rows, and the test error falls to nineteen thousand nine hundred and twenty five pounds, a third of the baseline. Cell twenty prints what the model learned: one number per feature. And now, the reveal I promised at the start. Millbrook is synthetic. Its prices were made by a rule, written in the generator script, and kept out of every scene until now. The rule says: a hundred and twenty pounds per square foot, nine thousand pounds per garage space, six thousand per step of condition, a premium per area, all in January twenty twenty one money, with the market rising by zero point three five percent a month. Halfway through the period, that rise is a factor of about one point one three. The table puts the model beside the rule at that point. One hundred and thirty six pounds per square foot against one hundred and thirty five. Garages, ten and a half thousand against ten thousand one hundred. Riverside over Eastfield, sixty nine thousand against sixty seven and a half. And built and bedrooms, which are not in the rule at all, come out close to zero. The model never saw the rule. It found it in fourteen hundred noisy sales.

In the visualisation course, prices looked symmetric on a log scale, and I suggested a model on log prices might do better, because it makes errors in percentages. That was a hypothesis. This section tests it. Cell twenty one wraps the same pipeline in a transformed target regressor: it fits on the log of price, and converts its predictions back with exp. To compare the two fairly in percentage terms, typical miss measures each house's error as a share of its price, and takes the median. The linear model on price misses by six point two percent. The log model, by seven percent. Worse. Cell twenty two splits the test houses into thirds by price and compares the median error in each. The log model wins only on the cheapest third, by a few hundred pounds, and loses on the rest. So we drop it. And there is a reason, which the reveal from the last section explains. These prices were built by adding pounds: so much per square foot, plus so much per garage, plus the area premium. A straight line in pounds is exactly the right shape for that. Real markets are often more multiplicative, and then the log target would win. The lesson is the loop in the side pane. An idea, however sensible, is a hypothesis. Measure it on the test set, then keep it or drop it, and say which.

A completely different kind of model works by asking questions. Cell twenty three fits a decision tree, limited to three levels of questions. Its test error is thirty four thousand and eighty seven pounds, worse than the straight line on size alone. Cell twenty four prints the tree, and it is worth reading. The first question is about size: is it fifteen hundred and four square feet or less? The tree chose that question because, of all possible splits, it divides the prices most cleanly. Each side then asks about size again, at eleven hundred and twenty seven or two thousand and eighty four square feet. Then, mostly: is it in Riverside? So without being told anything, the tree found the two biggest effects in the data, size and Riverside, in the right order. Every house ends up in one of eight leaves, and each leaf predicts one price, the average of the training houses that landed there: from about a hundred and eighty nine thousand pounds to four hundred and eighty one thousand. That is the tree's weakness at this depth. It can only ever predict eight different prices, so a house at the edge of a box is valued like the middle of it. Trees shine where a line cannot follow the data, with thresholds and interactions. And their real power appears when many of them work together.

Gradient boosting is one of the most successful methods in practice for tables of data like ours, and the side pane gives the idea in three steps. A small tree makes its predictions, with errors. A second tree is trained to predict those errors, and its answer is used to correct the first, a little. A third tree predicts what is still wrong, and so on, a hundred times. Each tree is weak, and together they can follow almost any shape. Cell twenty five fits scikit learn's histogram based gradient boosting regressor, with a seed, and then puts every model so far on one leaderboard, scored on the same test houses. The median guess, fifty nine thousand pounds. The line on size, thirty two thousand. The decision tree, thirty four. The log model, twenty two thousand. Gradient boosting, twenty one thousand two hundred and ninety two. And the winner: the plain linear model with every feature, nineteen thousand nine hundred and twenty five pounds. That is a real result, and an important one. Boosting is not magic. These prices were built by adding effects together, which is exactly the shape a linear model assumes, so the linear model fits it best and boosting has nothing extra to find. On messier real data, with thresholds and interactions, the order would often flip. You find out by measuring, never by reputation.

Why stop the decision tree at three levels? Let it ask more questions and it should get better. Cell twenty six tests that, fitting trees from depth one to depth twenty, and scoring each twice: on the training rows it learned from, and on the test rows it has never seen. The table shows a few, and the plot on the right shows all twenty. The training error falls steadily, and at depth twenty it is fifteen pounds. Fifteen pounds! The tree has asked so many questions that almost every training house sits in its own leaf, so it simply repeats each house's price back. The test error tells the truth. It falls at first, from forty seven thousand at depth one to about thirty thousand at depth six, and then it rises again, to thirty three and a half thousand at depth twenty. The deep tree has learned the noise of the particular houses it was shown, details that do not repeat in new houses. That is overfitting: memorising the training data instead of learning the pattern. The gap between the two curves is the warning sign, and it is exactly why the test set exists. Depth is one of many settings like this, called hyperparameters, and choosing them well, without wearing out the test set in the process, is where the next course begins.

We have a winning model, and one test score. Two problems remain. One test set is a single exam, and a single exam can be lucky. And worse, every time we look at the test score to choose between models, a little of the test set leaks into our choices, until it is no longer an honest exam at all. Cross validation fixes both, using only the training rows. Cell twenty eight splits the training set into five folds, shuffled with a fixed seed. Then it trains the model five times. Each time, four fifths are used for training, and the remaining fifth is the exam. Every training row is examined exactly once. The side pane lists the five scores: between about twenty thousand and twenty two thousand pounds. Their mean, twenty thousand nine hundred and eighty one pounds, is the estimate of how the model will do on new houses, and their spread, about nine hundred pounds, says how much that estimate wobbles from one exam to another. The test score from the last course, nineteen thousand nine hundred and twenty five, sits comfortably inside that range, which is reassuring. From now on, every decision, which model, which settings, is made on these folds. The test set stays locked, for one final score at the very end.

Gradient boosting lost to the linear model, but it ran on its default settings. Perhaps it just needs tuning. Cell twenty nine sets up a grid search. It tries every combination of two settings: the learning rate, how much each new tree is allowed to correct, at three values, and the maximum number of leaves per tree, at three values. Nine combinations, each scored with the same five fold cross validation as before: forty five fits, all on the training rows. Cell thirty lists the best four. The winner is a learning rate of zero point one with at most seven leaves, with a cross validated error of twenty two thousand nine hundred and ten pounds. Cell thirty one puts it beside the linear model, both on the folds and on the test set. On the folds, the linear model wins, twenty thousand nine hundred and eighty one pounds against twenty two thousand nine hundred and ten. And on the test set, looked at once now that the choice is made, the linear model wins again, nineteen thousand nine hundred and twenty five against twenty thousand eight hundred and seventy four. Tuning improved boosting. It did not change the decision. And the decision was made on the folds, before the test set was consulted, which is what makes the test score still worth believing. The model to ship is the linear one.

A single error number hides where the errors are. Cell thirty two computes every test house's residual, the actual price minus the predicted one, and summarises it by area in two ways. The median error asks whether the model is biased, consistently too high or too low. The median miss asks how far off it is, in either direction. The side pane draws the bias as bars. In most areas, the median error is a couple of thousand pounds either way, close to zero, which is what an unbiased model should show. Old Town stands out: its houses sell for about six thousand nine hundred pounds more than the model predicts, consistently. That is not alarming, it is small next to Old Town's typical miss of about fourteen thousand pounds, and with only about fifty test houses per area some wobble is expected. But it is exactly the kind of thing to watch. If Old Town's under prediction grew as new sales arrived, it would mean something about Old Town that the model does not know, perhaps a new railway station, or the old town character itself. The next cell draws all the test errors as a histogram, on the right, centred near zero, roughly symmetric. A model you can trust has errors that look like noise: no pattern by area, by size, or by date.

Which features does the model actually rely on? Coefficients can mislead, because they depend on the units of each feature. Permutation importance asks the question directly, and it works for any model. The idea is in the side pane. Take the test set, and shuffle one column, say size, so that each house gets some other house's size. The link between that column and price is now broken. Score the model again, and see how much worse it gets. A column the model relies on costs a lot when it is shuffled. A column it ignores costs nothing. Cell thirty four does this for every column, twenty times each with a seed, and averages. Shuffling size adds fifty six thousand pounds to the error. Size is everything, as every course has hinted. Area adds twelve thousand, and months, the rising market, nine thousand four hundred. Garage, two thousand eight hundred, and condition about a thousand. And bedrooms and year built add nothing at all, within a few pounds of zero. That is the same conclusion as the coefficients and the hidden rule two sections ago, reached a completely independent way. When two different methods agree about what a model uses, you can explain it to someone with some confidence.

A valuation should come with how sure it is. One way is to train models for quantiles. Cell thirty five trains three boosted models, aimed at the tenth percentile, the median and the ninetieth percentile of price. Cell thirty six asks all three about one test house, fifteen hundred and sixty nine square feet in Hillcrest: two hundred and seventy one thousand, two hundred and ninety two thousand and three hundred and twelve thousand pounds. A ten to ninety percent interval, so it should contain the real price eighty percent of the time. This house actually sold for three hundred and twenty one thousand, outside it. That could be the one in five. So cell thirty seven checks the promise across every test house: the interval contains the price only sixty seven percent of the time. It promises eighty and delivers sixty seven. Its intervals are too narrow, overconfident. Cell thirty eight tries a simpler method. Take the linear model's own errors on the cross validation folds, houses it had not trained on, and use their tenth and ninetieth percentiles as the interval: minus thirty two thousand two hundred to plus thirty three thousand nine hundred pounds around each prediction. On the test set, that interval holds eighty four percent of prices: it keeps its promise, slightly cautiously. Always check whether an interval does what it says. This one is the interval we will ship.
