Every model has a region where it knows what it is talking about, and that region is the data it was trained on. Cell thirty nine asks about a house far outside it: a castle of twelve thousand square feet, built in sixteen fifty. The largest house the model has ever seen had three thousand eight hundred and thirty three square feet. The linear model carries on with its straight line and values the castle at one million, seven hundred and twenty five thousand pounds. The boosted trees value it at four hundred and sixty eight thousand, because trees cannot predict beyond the prices they have seen, so they simply flatten out. Two good models, two completely different answers, and neither should be believed. The side pane names the two zones. Inside the data, a model's predictions are as good as its validation said, within its interval. Outside it, the model is guessing, and the honest response is to refuse to answer. Cell forty shows the pipeline doing exactly that for one kind of question: an ordinary house in Harbourside, an area that is not in Millbrook's data. The one hot encoder has never seen it, and the prediction fails with a value error, found unknown categories. That is the right behaviour. In the last course, the command and the web service will turn both of these into clear messages instead of numbers.

The last check is about the work itself rather than the model: could someone else get exactly these numbers? Cell forty one prints the versions that produced every result in this course: Python three point fifteen point one, pandas three point one, NumPy two point five point four, scikit learn one point nine point one, all pinned in pyproject dot toml. A different version can change a default, a tie break, or a random number stream, and the numbers shift. The side pane lists the other half: every random step in this notebook was given a seed. The train test split, the cross validation folds, the trees, the boosting and the permutation importance all used random state fourteen sixty. And cell forty two scores the model once more: nineteen thousand nine hundred and twenty five pounds, exactly as before. That is not luck. Every notebook in this course, from the first cell of explore dot ipynb to here, is re run from top to bottom by the course's own checks, with a fresh kernel, a Restart and Run All, on every change, and every number on every screen is compared with what that run printed. Pins, seeds and a clean top to bottom run are what turn a notebook from something that worked once into a result other people can check. Next: taking it out of the notebook.

Everything so far lives in notebooks, which are perfect for asking questions and poor for running answers. A function defined in a notebook exists only inside one kernel. It cannot be imported by a script, tested, or used by a web service. So the last course moves the answers out of the notebooks and into a package, and the frame changes with it, from the notebook to the editor and terminal. The first thing to move is the cleaning. The editor shows house underscore prices slash clean dot py: the same clean function the cleaning course built in cell nineteen, now in a file, with one improvement, the area is title cased here too, so Old town can never come back. Underneath, a second function, load sales, reads an agency export and cleans it in one call. pyproject dot toml grows up to match: a build system section, the package's own dependencies, and the name of the package. Then pip install dash e dot installs the project into its own environment in editable mode, so any change to the file takes effect immediately. The terminal proves it works: a one line Python command imports load sales from the package, reads the raw export, and prints fourteen hundred and fifty three rows by ten columns. The notebook's answer, now from a module that anything can import.

The cleaning course found seven faults and fixed each one. A test makes sure each fix stays fixed. The editor shows tests slash test clean dot py, written for pytest, which this section adds to the project as a pinned development tool. At the top is one perfectly ordinary sale, written out as a dictionary, and a helper called raw that builds a one row raw export, with any changes you ask for. Each test then plants exactly one fault and asserts what clean must make of it. The highlighted one gives the price as pound two hundred and fifteen thousand, with the comma, and asserts that clean turns it into the number two hundred and fifteen thousand. The side pane lists every test beside the fault it guards and the section where we first met it: the day first dates, the square metre batch, the empty garages, the duplicates, the ten thousand pound transfer, and the area spellings. That last test is parametrised: pytest runs it three times, once for each spelling. In the terminal, pytest dash q runs them all: nine passed. Now suppose, months from now, someone tidies up clean and accidentally drops the comma handling. They will not find out from a wrong chart, weeks later. pytest will fail on the very next run, naming the fault that came back.

Next, the model. Two new modules hold what the modelling courses decided. features dot py names the seven features, computes months since January twenty twenty one, and builds the same column transformer as the notebook. train dot py, in the editor, does what the last three courses did, end to end, with no notebook in sight. It loads and cleans the raw export, makes the features, splits with the same seed, and fits the linear pipeline. Then it computes the interval offsets from cross validated errors, exactly as the trust course decided, and gathers the facts the model will need later into a small dictionary: its test error, the interval, the areas it knows, the range of sizes it learned from, and the latest month. joblib dot dump saves the fitted pipeline to models slash model dot joblib, and the facts go to model dot json beside it. The models folder is listed in dot gitignore, because a trained model is something to rebuild, not something to commit. In the terminal, python dash m house prices dot train runs it: eleven hundred and sixty two training sales, two hundred and ninety one test sales, and a test error of nineteen thousand nine hundred and twenty five pounds. The table on the right puts that beside the notebook's final score. Identical, to the pound. The package is the notebook, made repeatable.

Now the question the whole course has been asking finally gets a tool. Two more modules. value dot py loads the saved model and its facts, and holds the one function that matters: value, which takes a house, checks that it is inside the data the model knows, and returns a price with its interval, rounded to the nearest thousand. cli dot py, in the editor, wraps it in a command with argparse, and one line in pyproject, project dot scripts, turns house prices into a real command on the path. The terminal asks four questions. A seventeen hundred and ten square foot Riverside house, built in two thousand and four, with two garages: three hundred and eighty three thousand pounds, likely between three hundred and fifty and four hundred and seventeen thousand. The identical house in Eastfield: three hundred and thirteen thousand. Seventy thousand pounds less, just as the area coefficient said. Then the two questions from the trust course. A house in Harbourside: no valuation, because there are no sales in Harbourside, and the message lists the areas it does know. And the twelve thousand square foot castle: no valuation, because it learned from five hundred and twenty five to three thousand eight hundred and thirty three square feet. A clear refusal, with the reason, instead of a confident number that means nothing.

Agents rarely value one house at a time. A new file arrives in the data folder, listings dot csv: twenty houses for sale in Millbrook, with everything except a price. The command gains a second sub command, batch. The editor shows the function behind it, value file. It reads the listings, and for each house it fills the gaps the way the model expects: an empty garage means none, an unknown build year is left for the model's median. Then it calls exactly the same value function as before. If the house is one the model must refuse, the row gets a note explaining why, instead of a price. The batch never stops halfway, and it never invents a number. Finally it writes everything to a new file. In the terminal: house prices batch, data slash listings dot csv, dash dash out valued dot csv. Twenty houses valued. A quick look at the first few rows with cut and head shows the result, and the side pane draws it: each listing's id, area and size, followed by its price and the low and high ends of its interval. A Riverside house of twelve hundred and thirty nine square feet at about three hundred and three thousand pounds, a large Northgate house at three hundred and seventy nine thousand. That file could go straight into an agent's spreadsheet, or onto a website.

The last step puts the valuation behind a web address, so any app or website can ask for it. FastAPI and the uvicorn server join the project, pinned in their own dependency group. The editor shows the whole service in about twenty lines. House is a pydantic model: it declares each field and its type, and some rules, size must be positive, condition between one and five. FastAPI checks every incoming request against it before any of our code runs, and rejects bad input on its own. Below it, post value receives a checked house, calls the same value function as the command, and returns the price and interval as JSON. If value refuses, the service answers with status four twenty two and the reason. In the terminal, uvicorn starts the server in the background. Then curl sends two requests. A Riverside house of seventeen hundred and ten square feet with three bedrooms comes back as three hundred and sixty one thousand pounds, likely between three hundred and twenty nine and three hundred and ninety five thousand. It is lower than the command's valuation because this request says nothing about garages or build year, so the service assumes no garage. And a house in Harbourside gets a clear four twenty two, with the reason. Then pkill stops the server. Three front doors, a notebook, a command and an API, and one function behind them.

That is the whole journey. We started with a CSV of house sales that could not even be averaged, because one agent typed pound signs. We cleaned it fault by fault, and wrote down every fix. We grouped it, joined it, drew it honestly, and learned to say how sure we were, with intervals and fair tests, and to spot a confounder. We built features without leaking the answer, compared models against a baseline, and discovered that a simple straight line recovered the rule the data was made with. We validated it, checked that its interval kept its promise, and taught it to refuse what it does not know. And finally we shipped it, as a tested package, a command and a web service. On the left is what you have built. On the right is where each part grows next. Millions of sales instead of fourteen hundred mean tools like Spark and a lakehouse. Retraining every month, automatically, is a data pipeline, with tools like Airflow and dbt. More models, and why they work, is machine learning proper. Keeping a model honest in production, versioned, monitored, and watched for the kind of drift we saw in Old Town, is MLOps. And the statistics behind the bootstrap and the permutation test deserve a course of their own. Each of those has its own series on GraphL. Thanks for building this one with me.
